summary: Defines a MIB for managing the Baseline Privacy Interface, which provides data privacy for DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems and their termination systems, using SNMP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a dashboard for checking the privacy lock between a home cable modem and the cable company's equipment.

how is docsis bpi managed with snmp
subtitle: A set of SNMP-readable objects for watching and tuning the encryption keys of DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems.

tldr.problem: DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems and head-end equipment encrypt data with the Baseline Privacy Interface (BPI), but operators had no standard way to inspect or control its keys and state machines.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3083 defines the DOCS-BPI-MIB, an SNMPv2 (SMIv2) MIB module with one group of cable modem objects and one group of CMTS objects, built as an extension to the DOCSIS Radio Frequency Interface MIB, RFC 2670.
tldr.outcome: CableLabs requires this MIB in DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems that implement BPI. It does not cover BPI+, and it has since been updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3083 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 9141; it has not been obsoleted. It covers only the DOCSIS 1.0 Baseline Privacy Interface.

sections.title: What the MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 3083 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Baseline Privacy Interface (BPI). BPI is the DOCSIS specification that gives simple data privacy to DOCSIS 1.0 cable systems, and managing it is the whole focus of this document.

A cable modem (CM) is the subscriber-side station. The cable modem termination system (CMTS) sits in the head-end and is the master station. The MIB is meant to be read and written with SNMP, and it is written in SMIv2. It extends the DOCSIS Radio Frequency Interface MIB, RFC 2670.

The MIB is not enough for BPI+, the DOCSIS 1.1 specification that adds cable modem authentication. The working group expected to issue a separate MIB for that later.
sections.plainLanguage: A cable modem and the cable company's box talk in secret code. This note gives a list of dials and gauges so a technician can check that the secret code is working.

sections.title: Management Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists what operators need from the interface, and the MIB is shaped to meet it.

  • The CM and CMTS MUST support viewing relevant RSA public keys, for future subscriber authentication applications.
  • Operators need to configure the authorization and TEK finite state machine parameters, for performance tuning and security incident handling. The CMTS MUST support viewing (and configuring if possible) all of them, including whether baseline privacy is enabled, key lifetimes, key grace times and state timeouts. The CM MUST support viewing them where possible.
  • Operators need to analyze and override state machine behavior. The CM MUST support viewing the current states, and both devices MUST support viewing error codes and strings, counters for invalid key events, key expirations, renewals and duplicate messages, plus key sequence numbers and expiry times.
  • Operators need dynamic control of IP multicast distribution. The CMTS MUST support configuring and viewing all multicast forwarding state and group memberships within its MAC domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The technicians asked for gauges to see if the lock is healthy, dials to change how often the keys are swapped, and a guest list for who may watch the shared channels.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The MIB has one group of CM-only objects (docsBpiCmGroup) and one group of CMTS-only objects (docsBpiCmtsGroup).

On the cable modem there are two tables. docsBpiCmBaseTable holds basic privacy parameters and counters and manages the authorization state machine. docsBpiCmTEKTable manages the Traffic Encryption Key (TEK) state machine for each SID, the service identifier for a bidirectional security association.

On the CMTS there are four sub-groups: a base table, an authorization table with per-modem association information, a TEK table with per-SID information, and the multicast control tables. Two multicast tables work together. docsBpiIpMulticastMapTable maps downstream IP multicast traffic to multicast SIDs, and docsBpiMulticastAuthTable says which modems may receive each multicast SID. Together they limit multicast to authorized modems.

Some objects keep the older DisplayString and IpAddress conventions on purpose, to stay compatible with DOCSIS 1.0 modems that implemented earlier versions of the MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The modem has two notebooks, one for its main lock and one for each key it uses. The cable company's box has four, including a guest list for shared channels.

sections.title: Keys and State Machines
sections.content:
The key chain works like this. The CMTS sends the authorization key to the modem encrypted with the modem's RSA public key. The authorization key is used to derive a key encryption key, which protects the TEKs, and to derive message authentication keys. TEKs are used for DES encryption of upstream and downstream traffic.

Many objects reflect this. The modem's authorization state machine reports states such as authWait, authorized, reauthWait and authRejectWait. Grace time objects (1 to 1800 seconds) tell a modem how many seconds before a key expires it should start fetching a new one. Counters track requests, replies, rejects and invalids, and error code and error string objects record why a message was rejected.

Most objects are read-only on the modem. A few are writable: setting docsBpiCmAuthReset to TRUE generates a Reauthorize event in the authorization state machine, and reading it always returns FALSE.
sections.plainLanguage: The big lock opens a small box of keys, and the small keys scramble your data. If a key is about to run out, the modem starts asking for a new one early, and the gauges show how that is going.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank that BPI does not provide an authentication service. CMTS implementors are encouraged not to rely on a modem's MAC address for service authorization, in particular for docsBpiMulticastAuthTable. BPI+ does provide modem authentication.

The read-write objects should be protected from unauthorized modification to prevent denial of service and theft of service. The examples given are objects that reset state machines, change key lifetimes or grace times, and control multicast traffic.

The preferred protection is SNMPv3, using the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model. Weaker methods include the docsDevNmAccessTable from the Cable Device MIB and configuration-file options that disable SNMP SET operations at boot. These may be vulnerable to an unauthorized management station spoofing a legitimate station's source address.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can turn the dials could break the lock or sneak onto channels they did not pay for, so only trusted people should get the controls.
